title: Partridge

jokes.text: Ron is tricked by a process server using a fake free steak dinner offer, then served with a subpoena.
jokes.setup: A stranger claims Ron has won a free dinner from St. Elmo Steak House, knowing Ron's love of meat will make him reveal himself.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately breaks his stoic composure and announces himself — the one thing he'd do for a steak — and gets served.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy — the joke only works because the audience knows Ron's near-religious devotion to meat. It's perfectly structured: the setup feels innocuous, Ron's instant self-betrayal is the punchline, and it requires zero explanation. The process server's casual 'You've been served. Have a nice day.' lands as a deadpan bonus beat. High rewatch value because you can see it coming once you know the trick, which makes Ron's eagerness even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Process Server
dialogue.line: Ron, you've won a lifetime supply of bacon and prime rib!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm coming out!

dialogue.speaker: Process Server
dialogue.line: Wait, really? That easily?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Of course. Do you know me at all?

jokes.text: I don't like you. But I respect the effort.
jokes.setup: Ron has just been publicly outwitted and legally served.
jokes.punchline: Rather than being angry, Ron gives a grudging compliment — perfectly in character for a man who values competence above all.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. It's maximally economical — two short sentences that do enormous character work. Ron's worldview (competence earns respect regardless of personal feelings) is distilled into six words. Highly quotable, deeply Ron-specific, and the deadpan delivery makes it land without any inflation. This is what 8+ looks like for a line joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have to admit, I'm impressed. This is quality work. The forged signature, the official seal, the binding... whoever did this really knew what they were doing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Actually, wait. I did this. I'm impressed with myself.

jokes.text: $46 million for psychological damages. 'Yeah, that seems about accurate.'
jokes.setup: Ron reads the absurd breakdown of Jamm's lawsuit damages, culminating in $46 million for psychological damages.
jokes.punchline: Tom's instant, deadpan agreement — treating the insane number as reasonable — is the laugh.
jokes.explanation: Solid quick reaction beat. The escalating dollar amounts are funny on their own, but Tom's deadpan confirmation elevates it. Works because both the absurdity of the number and Jamm's awfulness are already established. Not especially original but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I went to the dentist last week. Reasonable costs, professional work. But then I got the bill for psychological damage from hearing the drill. $47,000.

jokes.text: We should sue Jamm's parents for spawning a human turdburger.
jokes.setup: The group is upset about Jamm's lawsuit.
jokes.punchline: April's characteristically caustic and creative insult — 'human turdburger' is an unusually specific and vulgar coinage.
jokes.explanation: Very April — the logical escalation of suing Jamm's parents for creating him, paired with the inventive compound insult 'turdburger,' gets a solid laugh. Character-specific but not exceptional craft.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Forty-six million dollars in psychological damage? That seems fair. I once spilled coffee on myself and I think that was worth at least three million.

jokes.text: Ron declines Andy as attorney, saying he represents himself 'in all legal matters and livestock auctions.'
jokes.setup: Andy enthusiastically offers to be Ron's lawyer with a strategy of objecting to everything.
jokes.punchline: Ron's dignified refusal reveals that his preferred self-representation extends to livestock auctions — an absurdly specific detail that perfectly characterizes his frontier self-reliance.
jokes.explanation: The 'livestock auctions' addition is the key — it's not just that Ron is self-reliant, it's the specificity of the world he inhabits. Could only be Ron. Excellent economy and character integration. The 'and livestock auctions' tag is a perfectly calibrated absurdist escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Counter-sue his parents for creating a human turdburger.

jokes.text: I wish we had $46 million. We could buy my parents' house and evict them.
jokes.setup: Discussion of the enormous lawsuit figure.
jokes.punchline: April immediately fantasizes about using a hypothetical windfall to evict her own parents — a dark, specific, and perfectly April non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: April's nihilistic family relationship is a recurring character beat, and this is a good, quick deployment of it. The pivot from sympathizing with Ron to fantasizing about her parents' eviction is funny in its self-interest. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I will be representing myself in court. I've studied the law extensively.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Legal proceedings are not unlike a livestock auction. You make your case, the judge decides, and someone goes home unhappy.

jokes.text: Surprised he's taking it this well. [Ron immediately destroys something offscreen with a crash]
jokes.setup: Tom comments that Ron seems calm about the lawsuit.
jokes.punchline: Immediately after, a loud crash — Ron has clearly destroyed something. The visual gag is the instantaneous contradiction of Tom's observation.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom ironic cut — the line 'surprised he's taking it this well' is instantly demolished by the crash. Well-structured and perfectly timed. The economy is exceptional (setup delivered verbally, punchline entirely physical). Not highly original as a technique but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? If I had a million dollars, my first instinct would be to evict my parents from their house and then buy it back.

jokes.text: 'April, could you call maintenance please?' — Ron calmly asks after his outburst
jokes.setup: Ron has just destroyed something in apparent rage
jokes.punchline: Immediate return to bureaucratic normalcy — Ron's emotional outburst is followed by a perfectly composed administrative request
jokes.explanation: The immediate pivot from violent rage to calm administrative competence is a perfect Ron button. It suggests he has done this before and has a system. Extremely economical — five words do all the work. Strong character integration: only Ron transitions from destruction to office protocol this smoothly.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm handling this lawsuit very maturely. I've accepted that sometimes life throws curveballs and you just have to roll with the punches.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: THAT IS A GODDAMN LIE! THIS IS AN OUTRAGE! I WILL BURN THIS ENTIRE SYSTEM DOWN!

jokes.text: Leslie finds the exact spot where 18-year-old Ben was inaugurated and gets chills. Ben awkwardly thanks people passing by.
jokes.setup: Leslie is emotionally invested in the historical significance of Ben's childhood inauguration spot.
jokes.punchline: Ben has no idea what to do with Leslie's enthusiasm and defaults to thanking random people — his nervousness and her intensity create the comic friction.
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy playing off their well-established dynamic — Leslie's obsessive enthusiasm vs. Ben's self-deprecating awkwardness. Gets the scene going but isn't especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben is such a better mayor than all the other mayors. He's more organized, more efficient, more decisive...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And he has really nice arms.

jokes.text: None of the other mayors had as cute a butt as you do. / And none of them caused the city's unemployment rate to hit 30%.
jokes.setup: Leslie is romanticizing Ben's past as mayor with a compliment about his butt.
jokes.punchline: Ben deadpans back the actual dark fact — 30% unemployment — subverting Leslie's romantic reframing.
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline. Leslie's butt compliment is itself funny, and Ben's pivot to the unemployment rate is well-timed self-deprecation. Shows both characters well.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did you know that unemployment is at 8.3%?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, stop. You're getting me so hot right now.

jokes.text: You're so sexy when you talk about percentages.
jokes.setup: Ben has just mentioned the 30% unemployment disaster he caused.
jokes.punchline: Leslie finds even his failures attractive — the joke is that 'percentages' is perhaps the least sexy thing imaginable, but Leslie Knope would absolutely be turned on by civic data.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character integration — this joke requires knowing that Leslie Knope is turned on by government and data. Short, punchy, and lands perfectly. Could only be said by Leslie and only land because of who she is. Just below the 8 threshold because it's a one-liner without the structural complexity of the top jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Oh, here comes Ron Swanson, the man himself. Or should I say... Ron Spam-son!

jokes.text: Well, if it isn't the defendant, Ron Swansuck.
jokes.setup: Jamm opens his confrontation with Ron.
jokes.punchline: 'Swansuck' — Jamm's childish name-alteration insult — establishes his petty, juvenile character while being inherently funny in its lameness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that 'Swansuck' is a terrible insult — it works because it's meant to characterize Jamm as a petulant child. The humor is meta: we laugh at how bad the joke is, and that badness is the point. Functional character-establishing comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This lawsuit is absolutely ridiculous. It's like 'Legally Blonde' meets 'Ridiculously Expensive.'

jokes.text: This lawsuit is Chronicles of Riddick-ulous.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to express that the lawsuit is ridiculous.
jokes.punchline: He mashes 'Chronicles of Riddick' and 'ridiculous' into a portmanteau — a very Tom-specific brand of pop-culture wordplay.
jokes.explanation: Tom's pop-culture-portmanteau wordplay is his signature comedic voice, and 'Chronicles of Riddick-ulous' is a genuinely good example of it. Character-specific and has a nice groan-worthy quality. Not groundbreaking but well-executed Tom Haverford humor.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I have a complaint about the city's healthcare policies and the unprofessional conduct of the nursing staff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Jeremy, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: That nurse at the city clinic, she's clearly a lesbian.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? How is that relevant to anything?

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, she didn't appreciate my advances, which is discrimination against heterosexual men.

jokes.text: Jamm lists grievances: 'This munch throws me into a swimming pool. The nurse still won't have sex with me, and she's not even queer.'
jokes.setup: Jamm is explaining his motivation for the lawsuit.
jokes.punchline: His grievances escalate from legitimate (being thrown in a pool) to the deeply pathetic revelation that Ann Perkins won't sleep with him, with the added detail 'and she's not even queer' — indicating he's used that excuse before.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from being physically assaulted to 'the nurse won't sleep with me' as a comparable grievance is great character comedy. The 'not even queer' addition implies Jamm has a whole excuse system for rejection — it's pathetic and revealing in equal measure. Good Jamm character work.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: That's a Jamm family saying.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's just a common phrase that everyone says.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: No, my family invented it.

jokes.text: It's what we in the Jamm family call 'payback time.' / 'Everyone calls it that.' / 'Yeah, because I invented it.'
jokes.setup: Jamm announces his proprietary family phrase.
jokes.punchline: Tom deflates it immediately; Jamm doubles down by claiming to have invented the phrase 'payback time' — an absurd claim delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure is perfect: setup (proprietary phrase), deflation (everyone says that), absurd escalation (I invented it). Jamm's unearned self-importance is the engine of his character and this is a crisp deployment of it. Tom's one-line deflation is exactly the right weight.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: My lawyer says I don't have no case.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's lawyers once got him $60,000 because 'he got too scared at a haunted house'
jokes.setup: Tom warns that Jamm is using Jean-Ralphio's lawyers, who are dangerously good
jokes.punchline: Their most notable victory: $60,000 for Jean-Ralphio being frightened at a haunted house
jokes.explanation: A perfect piece of world-building comedy. The haunted house lawsuit is both absurd and oddly believable in the Parks universe. It also perfectly characterizes Jean-Ralphio as someone who would do this. The detail is specific enough to feel like a real case and funny enough to land hard. The groan from the group is the natural audience surrogate reaction.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Jean-Ralphio's lawyers got him a settlement from a haunted house because he was actually scared.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, that's what haunted houses are supposed to do.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, but he sued them for emotional distress. He won fifty thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's insane. How is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: His lawyer argued that the haunted house was too haunted.

jokes.text: Maybe not, but I'm not not going to win nothing.
jokes.setup: Tom tells Jamm he won't win $50 million.
jokes.punchline: Jamm responds with a triple negative that, parsed, means 'I will definitely win something' — but delivered with the confidence of someone who thinks he's being clever while actually being grammatically incoherent.
jokes.explanation: The triple negative is a good Jamm joke — he's trying to sound threatening while accidentally undermining himself linguistically. Plays well in the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I won the gardening contest!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's amazing! Who did you compete against?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, technically just myself. I was the only entry.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, that's not winning a contest, that's just having a garden.

jokes.text: You can win at anything. Last year I won an organic gardening contest. / Who were you competing against? / My own taste buds.
jokes.setup: Ann tells Chris you can't win a co-parenting compatibility quiz. Chris insists you can win at anything and cites an organic gardening contest.
jokes.punchline: When asked who he competed against, the answer 'my own taste buds' — a competition with no external opponent, judged entirely internally — is both absurdist and perfectly Chris.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is impeccable: Chris's manic positivity leads him to claim victory in a 'contest' where he is both the participant and the judge, which is philosophically absurd but tonally perfect for Chris. 'My own taste buds' is a genuinely surprising and original punchline. High quotability, high originality, and only Chris Traeger could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Chris, we scored a 94% compatibility match. That's basically a soulmate indicator.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Tom, that's just a fun test. It doesn't mean anything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Doesn't mean anything? Chris, we need to combine our genetics immediately. I'm talking a beautiful Treat-Perkins hybrid. We'd create the most efficient, most well-intentioned human ever born.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Tom, no.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Our child would run a 6-minute mile while solving world hunger. It's science.

jokes.text: Ann reveals she wants to have a baby and Chris has agreed to be the father. 'If this were the '80s, all we'd have to do is not drop an egg for a whole day. Stupid internet.'
jokes.setup: Ann explains their co-parenting compatibility quiz context.
jokes.punchline: Her nostalgic reference to the classic egg-baby exercise — and frustration that the internet has made parental assessment more sophisticated — is a funny, relatable aside.
jokes.explanation: Mildly charming observational aside. 'Stupid internet' is a good button but the joke overall is more pleasant than sharp. The egg-baby nostalgia is relatable but the joke doesn't have a strong enough punchline to land big.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, I think this is actually great news. We failed the compatibility test, which means we're compatible with failure. And failure is just success that hasn't happened yet. So really, we're succeeding at failing, which means we're winning.

jokes.text: 58% compatibility. 'I think it's literally the best score we could have hoped for.' / 'Not sure that that's true.'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann get a 58% co-parenting compatibility score.
jokes.punchline: Chris's reflexive positivity leads him to declare it 'literally the best score we could have hoped for' — which Ann drily corrects. The joke is the gap between Chris's optimism and reality.
jokes.explanation: Efficient Chris character joke. His 'literally the best score we could have hoped for' is classic Chris Traeger positive spin on objectively mediocre news, and Ann's deadpan correction is well-timed. The 'not sure that that's true' understatement works.

dialogue.speaker: Stephanie
dialogue.line: So now that you're marrying Ben, I guess that makes us sisters!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know! I'm so excited!

jokes.text: Tom reveals he also took the quiz for fun and got 81% with Chris. 'You wanna make a baby, Traeger? Your hair, my everything else. That kid would be unstoppable.'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann are disappointed by their 58% score when Tom casually reveals he and Chris scored 81%.
jokes.punchline: Tom's proposition — 'your hair, my everything else' — is a wonderfully confident and absurd co-parenting pitch, perfectly Tom.
jokes.explanation: Tom's intrusion into Chris and Ann's emotional moment with his unsolicited quiz result is a great comedic beat. The specificity of 'your hair, my everything else' is pure Tom — self-aggrandizing, oblivious to the moment, and inherently funny. Good structure with the escalating compatibility reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So tell me about Ben's sexual history. I want to know everything. Was he a late bloomer? Did he have any weird phases? Any unusual requests in the bedroom?

dialogue.speaker: Ben's Sister
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm not doing this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on, I'm trying to bond with you! This is what sisters do, right?

jokes.text: Ben's sister reveals she also took the quiz — Ben and Ann score 84%. 'Well, this sucks.' / 'Yes, we did not win.'
jokes.setup: Tom has already upstaged Chris and Ann with 81%; Ben's sister adds another reveal.
jokes.punchline: The escalating quiz scores turn the co-parenting test into an absurd competition. Chris's '...yes, we did not win' is a perfect deadpan button.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the quiz score gag is well-constructed, turning a straightforward B-plot into a comedic competition. 'Yes, we did not win' is a great Chris Traeger line — his relentlessly positive framing even in defeat. The callback to his earlier 'winning' philosophy adds resonance.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The judge asked me if I had any prior convictions, and I said, 'Your Honor, I can't even trust my own testimony.'

jokes.text: Leslie asks if Ben had a bossy older brother and made him watch Star Wars. Ben's sister: 'Make me? I loved those movies just as much as he did.'
jokes.setup: Leslie probes Ben's childhood with the assumption that Star Wars was a forced sibling burden.
jokes.punchline: Stephanie deflates the assumption — she was an equal Star Wars nerd, which reveals Ben's geekiness runs in the family.
jokes.explanation: Mild character beat that adds to Ben's established nerd identity. Pleasant but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron's not violent. He's actually a vegetarian.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I am not a vegetarian. I love meat.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You love the idea of meat. But you're too much of a pacifist to actually kill an animal yourself.

jokes.text: Leslie has a binder on Ben. 'Who were Ben's high school girlfriends and what base do you think he got to?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is interviewing Ben's sister, ostensibly for the ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has a binder — of course she does — and is asking invasive questions about Ben's romantic history. The juxtaposition of her organizational thoroughness with her jealousy/curiosity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The binder is a perfect Leslie prop — her obsessive preparation applied to jealous romantic reconnaissance. The 'what base do you think he got to?' question is funny because of the institutional formality she brings to an invasive personal question.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, you're so gentle and kind. I'm going to start calling you 'Snugglebottom.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, never do that again.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Too late. Snugglebottom's already out there.

jokes.text: Andy's testimony: 'Defendant, alias Ron Swanson, alias my boss, used appropriate force to prevent further damage to the wedding of Leslie Knope, alias my other boss.'
jokes.setup: Andy is giving formal court testimony.
jokes.punchline: His attempt at legalese collapses into 'alias my boss' and 'alias my other boss' — the 'alias' is used incorrectly, revealing Andy's misunderstanding of legal terminology while also being somehow endearing.
jokes.explanation: Andy trying to do formal legal language and reducing his understanding of the principals to 'my boss' and 'my other boss' is very Andy. The use of 'alias' for people he personally knows is a good malapropism joke. Well-integrated into character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your Honor, I'm here to testify that... actually, I just need to say, that suit is absolutely immaculate. The tailoring, the fabric, the way it drapes. Where did you get it? Because I need to know immediately. And those shoes? Italian leather? They're perfect. I'm not even sure what case we're discussing anymore, but whoever hired this lawyer made an excellent decision based purely on their aesthetic choices.

jokes.text: Andy reveals he failed the police brain exam. 'Well, I pooched the brain exam. Just to be safe, I wouldn't take anything I say too seriously.'
jokes.setup: Andy mentions his interest in law enforcement and that he was deemed unfit for the force.
jokes.punchline: He advises the court not to take his testimony seriously — which is itself testimony, making it self-defeating. 'Pooched' is also a great word choice.
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. Andy's self-deprecating disclosure that his testimony shouldn't be trusted — while on the stand, giving testimony — is a delightful logical paradox. 'Pooched the brain exam' is an excellent phrase. The structure is circular and funny. High character integration — only Andy would volunteer this information.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I hate lying. I hate it so much that I'd rather take a roundhouse kick to the face from a hippie than sit through someone's lies. And skim milk is the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If you're not going to give me the fat, just give me water. Why would you even bother?

jokes.text: April testifies that Ron is like 'a big, old, soft teddy bear' whose office nickname is 'Softy-pants McHuggable.'
jokes.setup: April is asked if she's ever heard Ron threaten to hurt anyone.
jokes.punchline: April invents the most anti-Ron characterization imaginable — 'vegetarian,' 'teddy bear,' 'Softy-pants McHuggable' — all of which are essentially slander for Ron Swanson, who is none of these things.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke because it works on two levels: (1) April's flat-affect delivery of the most absurd anti-Ron characterization is funny on its own, and (2) for anyone who knows Ron Swanson, each descriptor is maximally wrong. 'Softy-pants McHuggable' is an inspired coinage. The cut to Ron's likely horrified reaction (noted by his later comment about being called a vegetarian) adds further dimension.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That speech was beautiful, Ben. You made me cry. First because it was so touching and personal, then because I realized that everything we do is meaningless in the vast expanse of the universe, and we're all just tiny specks of dust hurtling through the void toward inevitable death.

jokes.text: April asks to see the judge's pocket square mid-testimony: 'Also, may I say for the record, that is a dope pocket square. Can I see that bad boy?'
jokes.setup: April is delivering formal testimony in court.
jokes.punchline: She abruptly pivots from legal testimony to complimenting and requesting the judge's pocket square — a completely unhinged courtroom move, fully in character for April.
jokes.explanation: April's total disregard for courtroom decorum, expressed through a fashion compliment to the judge, is a great beat. Her mode of subversion — not anger or defiance but bored enthusiasm for accessories — is very specifically April. 'Can I see that bad boy?' mid-testimony is delightfully absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why is this happening to me? I eat right, I exercise, I don't even drink that much.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You have a kidney stone.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A kidney stone? How is that possible? I'm a man.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional: Tom and April lied in court. 'There's only one thing I hate more than lying. Skim milk. Which is water that's lying about being milk.'
jokes.setup: Ron acknowledges his witnesses lied, then says there's only one thing he hates more than lying.
jokes.punchline: 'Skim milk. Which is water that's lying about being milk.' — a perfectly Ron definition that turns a dietary preference into a philosophical statement about deception.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the great Ron Swanson lines in the series. The structure is perfect: Ron sets up a ranking ('there's only one thing I hate more than lying'), which creates the expectation of something important, then subverts it with a petty food preference. But the definition — 'water that's lying about being milk' — elevates it from a simple misdirection to a genuine philosophical statement in Ron's voice. It's maximally economical, originaly, character-specific, and instantly quotable. Comparable to the anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I think I'm in labor! Oh my god, oh my god!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you're not in labor. You just ate a whole pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm serious! I can feel it! And there's two of them!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Two what?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Twins! I'm having twins!

jokes.text: Leslie asks 'Are you crying again?' — Ben has been crying repeatedly before the ceremony.
jokes.setup: Leslie catches Stephanie emotional again about Ben's speech.
jokes.punchline: 'Again' implies this has happened multiple times — the running gag of Stephanie's overwhelming emotion about Ben's homecoming.
jokes.explanation: Light running gag beat. Stephanie's excessive emotion about Ben is a mild but consistent comic element. The 'again' does a lot of work efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're so beautiful. You're like a smart, beautiful, talented... binglebop.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Your eyes are like two sparkly... shrimps. And your hair smells like... nectarines and persimmons.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You make me feel all... flibberflabber.

jokes.text: Stephanie cries at Ben's speech because she thinks about 'where you've been and where you're going and our future children and America and just our history as a nation.'
jokes.setup: Stephanie is explaining why she cries at Ben's speech.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from personal to national to continental — 'America' and 'our history as a nation' are completely disproportionate to a small-town key ceremony, revealing Stephanie's emotional overflow.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from personal sentiment to national history is a solid comedic list. The absurdity of connecting Ben's small-town key ceremony to 'our history as a nation' is funny. Moderate craft.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: You need to stay in the hospital for at least another night, Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: We need to monitor you closely.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I feel fine, really.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, but those are the rules, Binder.

jokes.text: Ben doubled over in pain, groaning, convinced he is 'giving birth.' 'I think I'm giving birth. Is that possible? No, right?' / 'It's twins!'
jokes.setup: Ben is extremely nervous before the ceremony (having gone to the bathroom five times).
jokes.punchline: He collapses in kidney stone pain and his morphine-addled hospital behavior is set up here with 'It's twins!' — his complete misread of what's happening to him.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of Ben collapsing is set up well by his nervous bathroom visits. 'It's twins!' is a decent button on the scene — using the pregnancy parallel as a closing joke. Not highly original but functional physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I can't believe I forgot the eggs at the grocery store. I basically abandoned babies.

jokes.text: Ben on morphine: 'Leslie and Dr. Clipperton — wow, man, I'm so glad you guys are meeting. It's like worlds collide. You know, I love it. I want candy.'
jokes.setup: Ben is on morphine after his kidney stone diagnosis.
jokes.punchline: His stream-of-consciousness delight at a mundane meeting, capped by the non-sequitur 'I want candy,' establishes the morphine-Ben comedy engine.
jokes.explanation: 'I want candy' as an out-of-nowhere pivot from emotional social observation is a good morphine joke. The worlds-colliding framing for something trivial is funny. Sets up the morphine-Ben bit well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I crushed that testimony. The judge was hanging on my every word.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I even referenced 'The Social Network' — or as I call it, TSN — to illustrate my point about digital entrepreneurship.

jokes.text: Morphine Ben calls Leslie a 'snug-bug' or 'snugger-doodle or something like that.'
jokes.setup: Morphine Ben is trying to express how beautiful Leslie is.
jokes.punchline: His drug-addled brain invents the words 'snug-bug' and 'snugger-doodle' as terms of endearment — the invented words are funny precisely because they're so uncertain and soft.
jokes.explanation: The invented words 'snug-bug' and 'snugger-doodle' are good absurdist comedy — the uncertainty ('or something like that') makes it land better. Morphine Ben is a reliable comedic device and this is a solid early deployment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, I don't appreciate you lying to me. You told me you were a vegetarian.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I am a vegetarian.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A vegetarian. I don't know what kind of sick game you're playing, but I will not be spoken to that way.

jokes.text: Morphine Ben wants to make his speech to the crowd and says he'll 'explain that love is everywhere and they have to surrender to the flow of the universe.' Then: 'Price is Right is on, I think.'
jokes.setup: Morphine Ben insists on delivering his speech despite being hospitalized.
jokes.punchline: His proposed speech philosophy has elevated to cosmic levels, then immediately deflates with 'Price is Right is on, I think' — the perfect morphine attention span.
jokes.explanation: The 'Price Is Right' pivot from cosmic philosophy is a great morphine beat. The escalation of Ben's speech plan to 'surrender to the flow of the universe' followed immediately by 'The Price Is Right is on' is a well-structured comedic reversal. Adam Scott plays drug-addled well.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't understand why everyone cares so much about honesty. I'm honest all the time and nobody likes me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not honesty, that's just being mean.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Same thing.

jokes.text: Ann forgot the eggs at the Kroger. 'I bought 12 babies, and then I immediately abandoned them at a Kroger's.'
jokes.setup: Chris has brought eggs as baby substitutes for the co-parenting exercise; Ann reveals she left them at the store.
jokes.punchline: 'I bought 12 babies and then I immediately abandoned them at a Kroger's' — Ann's reframing of the egg abandonment in worst-possible parenting terms is an excellent self-own.
jokes.explanation: This is a great line. The reframing of 'I forgot the eggs' as 'I abandoned 12 babies at a Kroger's' is a perfect comedic translation — taking the egg-baby metaphor to its logical extreme and turning it into a self-indictment. 'A Kroger's' is also a funny specific choice. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Lying is all I know. I was born under the bridge, raised by wolves, won a game show, and married a beautiful woman I met in the slums.

jokes.text: Tom compares his courtroom testimony to 'Mark Z in the Social N,' meaning Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network.
jokes.setup: Tom is proud of his lying testimony and comparing himself to a cultural touchstone.
jokes.punchline: He refers to Zuckerberg and The Social Network via the abbreviation 'Mark Z in the Social N' — peak Tom Haverford cultural name-dropping with maximum economy.
jokes.explanation: Tom's cultural reference compression is a signature bit. 'Mark Z in the Social N' is a decent example — the abbreviation implies he's too busy/cool to say full names. Solid Tom character joke, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I gotta tell you, I've been feeling great lately! Like, really great. My digestion has been on point, my bowels are moving like clockwork, and I'm not even gonna lie, some of my poops have been absolutely pristine. Perfect geometry, man. I'm talking museum-quality specimens here.

jokes.text: Ron: 'You even called me a... [whispers] vegetarian. What if that testimony leaks? How will people ever respect me?'
jokes.setup: Ron is upset that Tom and April lied in court. His primary concern is addressed.
jokes.punchline: Ron whispers 'vegetarian' as if it's the most shameful possible thing — more damaging to his reputation than the lawsuit itself.
jokes.explanation: Ron's horror at being labeled a vegetarian — whispered with the gravity of a slur — is a perfect callback and outstanding character integration. For Ron Swanson, being called a vegetarian is a worse reputation damage than a $46 million lawsuit. The whisper is crucial to the delivery. Genuinely funny character moment that works as a callback to April's testimony.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what? Jazz is just... it's beautiful, man. It's like... it's like everyone's playing their own song, but somehow it all comes together. That's society, you know? We're all just improvising, and somehow it works.

jokes.text: April: 'The truth is stupid. I only tell the truth when it makes me sound like I'm lying.'
jokes.setup: Ron is lecturing Tom and April about their perjury.
jokes.punchline: April's anti-truth philosophy — 'I only tell the truth when it makes me sound like I'm lying' — is a beautifully constructed, logically consistent statement of her worldview.
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. 'I only tell the truth when it makes me sound like I'm lying' is a paradoxical statement that is also a perfect encapsulation of April Ludgate's character — she performs deception as an identity. The sentence is structurally elegant and highly quotable. One of the episode's best character lines alongside the skim milk joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you know the mascot protocol?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I may have eaten an entire pan of hash brownies, but I still remember that the mascot can never break character in front of children, and if the head falls off, you have to kick it out of the room like it's on fire.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Lying is all I know. It's how I was able to scrape by on the streets of Bombay and make it on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire and get reunited with the love of my life, Latika.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains his relationship with lying.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a completely straight Slumdog Millionaire synopsis as if it's his personal autobiography — a perfect reference that works because Tom Haverford would absolutely plagiarize a movie's backstory.
jokes.explanation: A strong pop culture joke that actually works: Tom is of South Asian descent (his birth name is Tahir Haverford) and he appropriates the entire Slumdog Millionaire plot as personal biography — which lands because Tom would absolutely do this. The joke respects both the character and the reference, using the movie's specifics (Bombay, Latika, the game show) for maximum recognition. The commitment to the full plot synopsis rather than a single reference is the right comedic choice.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've never met Jeremy Jamm.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But I want to punch him based solely on his appearance.

jokes.text: Andy's 'truth bomb': 'Sometimes when I blow my nose, I get a boner. I don't know why. It just happens. Truth bomb.'
jokes.setup: Ron is praising Andy for telling the truth even when it was humiliating. Andy demonstrates his commitment to truth-telling.
jokes.punchline: Andy volunteers the most unnecessary, personal, physiologically baffling truth possible as evidence of his honesty — the 'truth bomb' tag is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Andy's unfiltered over-sharing is his defining characteristic, and 'sometimes when I blow my nose I get a boner' is a perfect application: it's specific, deeply strange, delivered with total sincerity, and the 'truth bomb' sign-off elevates it. The joke is earned because it builds on Ron's praise of Andy's honesty — this is Andy demonstrating what honest looks like for him. High impact, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You should have just hit him with a rock.

jokes.text: Tom and April refuse in unison: both: NO! — when Ron tells them to recant perjury. Ron sighs: 'They are so young. So much to learn.'
jokes.setup: Ron tells Tom and April to recant their perjured testimony.
jokes.punchline: Their synchronized 'NO!' followed by Ron's weary parental wisdom — 'so much to learn' — positions Ron as a disappointed but fond authority figure.
jokes.explanation: A nice ensemble beat. Ron's weary 'they are so young, so much to learn' after his young colleagues refuse to do the ethical thing is good character comedy — ironic given that the lesson is 'don't commit perjury,' which shouldn't require wisdom to understand.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no! It says 'Ice Clown'! It's supposed to say 'Ice Town'!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's fine. It's just a banner.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It is NOT fine! Ice Town was your vision! Your legacy! And now everyone thinks you're the Ice Clown!

jokes.text: Jamm watches Ben's hospital video: 'I feel like I never gave Miles Davis proper shrift. Like, I just didn't get into it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie shows Jamm video proof that Ben is hospitalized, not faking illness.
jokes.punchline: Morphine Ben's video rambling lands on an earnest mid-grade jazz confession — 'I never gave Miles Davis proper shrift' is the perfect drug-addled non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Morphine Ben's Miles Davis revelation is a good absurdist beat — the specificity of 'proper shrift' and the admission that he just 'didn't get into it' is exactly the kind of regret that occupies morphine brain. Works as proof-of-hospitalization comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mayor Stice
dialogue.line: This key represents the frozen heart of our great city. Just like this ice, my leadership is cold, unforgiving, and will eventually melt away into nothing, leaving only a puddle of regret and broken promises.

jokes.text: Ben on the phone from hospital: 'I'm Goodie Goodie. You just do your thing, baby Smurf.'
jokes.setup: Leslie calls from Partridge to check on Ben.
jokes.punchline: Morphine Ben gives an all-clear using 'Goodie Goodie' and calling Leslie 'baby Smurf' — invented terms of endearment in the tradition of 'snugger-doodle.'
jokes.explanation: Running morphine-Ben gag continues. 'Baby Smurf' is a good addition to his morphine vocabulary. Consistent execution of the established bit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben's not here today because he has a very serious medical condition. It's called... being awesome. And the symptoms are... leadership, intelligence, and a complete inability to gain weight no matter how much cake he eats. The prognosis? He's going to be fine. Better than fine. He's going to be great.

jokes.text: Ben hears 'Fred the Sled' is at the ceremony: 'They only bring him out for special occasions. I can't believe they're doing all this for me. The universe is love.'
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions the town mascot is at the ceremony. Ben perks up despite being high on morphine.
jokes.punchline: Ben's genuine pride in 'Fred the Sled' — a town mascot for a town that hates him — combined with his morphine conclusion 'the universe is love' is a good sad/funny beat.
jokes.explanation: Morphine Ben's hometown pride, enhanced by drugs, is bittersweet comedy. 'The universe is love' as a morphine conclusion is a good callback to his earlier cosmic philosophy bit. Moderate impact.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben is better than Judy Garland.

jokes.text: Tom recants perjury and the truth becomes a long, escalating list of times Ron said he wanted to punch Jamm. 'Which time? / Well, how many were there?'
jokes.setup: Tom agrees to recant his testimony and reveal the truth.
jokes.punchline: The implication is that Tom has so many instances to choose from that clarification is needed — which is both funny and bad for Ron's case.
jokes.explanation: Good structural beat — 'which time?' implying Ron's threats were too numerous to count is both funny and a plot escalation. Clean and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron's threats don't mean anything. He's all talk. Last week he threatened to 'dismantle the entire Parks Department from the inside,' and nothing happened. The week before that, he spent three days plotting to overthrow the government. It's basically his hobby at this point.

jokes.text: Jamm's dentist backstory: 'Yeah, we did a trade. I gave his wife new enamels, he gave my wife new yabbos.'
jokes.setup: Jamm is revealed through the testimony montage — people in Partridge meeting him and immediately wanting to punch him.
jokes.punchline: Jamm's casual disclosure of a barter arrangement — dental work for breast augmentation — using 'yabbos' is peak Jamm: sleazy, proud, and completely lacking self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's sleaziness is well-deployed here — the 'yabbos' barter is absolutely in character. Not structurally sophisticated but good Jamm characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have nothing but contempt for Jeremy Jamm. He is a pathetically weak man who would crumble under the slightest pressure. He's like a diver attempting a triple axel—he has no business being there, and when he inevitably fails, it will be tragic and embarrassing.

jokes.text: Random Partridge citizen meets Jamm and immediately: 'He looks like he could use a swift punch in the face though.'
jokes.setup: A random citizen in Partridge is asked to identify Jamm.
jokes.punchline: Without any context, upon mere sight of Jamm, this citizen volunteers that he looks like he deserves to be punched — confirming that Jamm's punchability is immediately apparent to strangers.
jokes.explanation: A great joke about the universal punchability of Jamm's face — the joke is that a complete stranger's first response to seeing Jamm is to want to punch him. It validates Ron's action retroactively and is a sharp, economical sight gag translated through dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have nothing to apologize for. I stand by every decision I've made.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And that's my final answer.

jokes.text: Second citizen: 'Bully for you. If it were me, I would have just punched him in the face.'
jokes.setup: Another Partridge citizen is telling a story about shoving Jamm into a pool.
jokes.punchline: His recommendation — 'I would have just punched him in the face' — is a callback to Ron's actual action while also being a running gag about how universally punchable Jamm is.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — the escalating testimony shows the whole town essentially validating Ron's punch. 'Bully for you' as a period-appropriate expression adds a small comic texture.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I'm going to coin a new term: 'self-jamm.' That's when you jam yourself.

jokes.text: Cut to Ron daydreaming at his desk: 'Just daydreaming about punching Jamm in the face.'
jokes.setup: The testimony montage reveals that multiple people have testified about Ron's desire to punch Jamm.
jokes.punchline: We cut to Ron at his desk, who confirms with complete serenity that he was daydreaming about exactly that — treated as a perfectly normal activity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic cut. The juxtaposition of earnest testimony about Ron's violent intentions with Ron himself calmly confirming it as casual daydreaming is excellent. Ron treating punching Jamm as a comfortable mental vacation is deeply in character. The economy is outstanding — five words do everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What do you want your future child to be?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I want him to be an Olympic biathlete who competes in the winter games, but only in the years that are divisible by four, and only if there's a full moon that week.

jokes.text: The banner at the Partridge ceremony reads 'ICE CLOWN' — the town has deliberately misspelled 'Ice Town' as an insult. Ben: 'That's a typo. That's a major typo. Oh, I'm just realizing that's not a typo.'
jokes.setup: Ben is watching via phone video as Leslie attends the ceremony, which is supposed to be a reconciliation.
jokes.punchline: The banner deliberately reads 'ICE CLOWN' — Ben's hope that it's a typo is immediately deflated when he processes that it's intentional. His real-time realization is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great joke. The visual gag of 'ICE CLOWN' — visible to the audience before Ben processes it — combined with Ben's real-time hope/disappointment is perfectly structured. 'I'm just realizing now that's not a typo' is an excellent deadpan realization. The joke captures the episode's emotional stakes (Ben finally getting closure) while being consistently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Van Dyne
dialogue.line: Well, based on what I'm seeing here, I'd say you two have virtually nothing in common. You don't like the same foods, you don't enjoy the same activities, you have completely different life goals. Frankly, I'm surprised you even know each other.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So... what are you saying?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Van Dyne
dialogue.line: I'm saying that statistically speaking, this relationship has about a 0.003% chance of success. You'll probably break up within the week, she'll take the apartment, you'll spiral into depression, lose your job, and end up living in your car.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Should we be concerned?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Van Dyne
dialogue.line: Very.

jokes.text: The key to the city is made of ice, and it melts in Leslie's hand. 'And it's water.' [crowd laughter]
jokes.setup: Leslie is accepting the key to the city on Ben's behalf.
jokes.punchline: The key is made of ice — a malicious metaphor made real — and it melts in her hand. The emcee explains: 'Much like the hopes and dreams of the people of Partridge, it melted away.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best bits. Making the key out of ice is a perfect vindictive prank — it's specific, creative, and devastating. The emcee's announcement connecting it to 'the hopes and dreams of the people of Partridge' elevates it from practical joke to performance art. The 'and it's water' reveal is a great punctuation. Excellent originality and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't measure my wealth in dollars. I measure it in pounds.

jokes.text: MC: 'Much like the hopes and dreams of the people of Partridge, it melted away. Again, this would all be way more satisfying if Ben was here.'
jokes.setup: The ice key has melted; the MC delivers an explanatory metaphor
jokes.punchline: Having delivered a devastating ceremonial indictment of Ben's legacy, the MC notes it would be 'way more satisfying' if Ben were there to experience the humiliation in person
jokes.explanation: The MC's complaint that his elaborate public humiliation has been robbed of its intended victim is a genuinely funny observation — the town prepared this whole show and Ben's kidney stones denied them their catharsis. The pathos of 'way more satisfying if Ben was here' is an unexpected emotional note.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Come on, buddy. Just take a bite.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, it's a statue.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're trying to feed it a sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: He looks hungry.

jokes.text: Leslie's defense of Ben includes: 'He's better than Judy Garland!' — crowd gasps. Leslie immediately: 'That's crazy. Judy Garland's amazing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie escalates her defense of Ben to claim he's better than every famous person from Partridge.
jokes.punchline: She claims Ben is better than Judy Garland, then immediately undercuts herself by acknowledging Judy Garland is amazing — caught between loyalty to Ben and objective reality.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's passionate over-advocacy colliding with her inherent honesty is perfect character comedy. The joke requires knowing that Leslie Knope is incapable of saying something she doesn't believe — so when she says Ben is better than Judy Garland, she has to immediately correct herself. 'That's crazy. Judy Garland's amazing.' is a great self-correction punchline. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've developed a compatibility test. Just one simple question that cuts through all the complexity.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Do you want to get a waffle?

jokes.text: Leslie's speech defending Ben: 'He has a calcified rock lodged in his penis!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is defending Ben's honor to the hostile Partridge crowd; she needs to prove he's legitimately ill
jokes.punchline: Leslie deploys the most graphic, clinical possible description of Ben's kidney stone location in a public speech — 'calcified rock lodged in his penis' — both oversharing and technically accurate
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'calcified rock lodged in his penis' — delivered in a public speech by someone trying to save face — is Leslie at her most unfiltered and well-intentioned. She's defending her husband with medical precision while inadvertently humiliating him in a different way. Very Leslie: correct and catastrophic simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Your stomach is really hard.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thanks, I've been working out.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, I mean... are you pregnant?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No! We just started trying.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Right, right. Sorry, I got ahead of myself.

jokes.text: Leslie concludes: 'Screw you, Partridge!' [crowd boos]
jokes.setup: Leslie has been trying to defend Ben's honor to an increasingly hostile Partridge crowd.
jokes.punchline: Her final defiant 'Screw you, Partridge!' is the inevitable conclusion of Leslie's escalating passion — she cannot contain herself and burns the bridge completely.
jokes.explanation: A good Leslie moment — her passion overriding her political judgment. 'Screw you, Partridge!' as the culmination of a speech that was supposed to be diplomatic is funny and character-consistent. The crowd booing is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ow! Ow! My back! My neck! Oh God, I can't feel my legs!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, I barely touched you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Barely touched me?! I'm going to need extensive physical therapy, possibly a wheelchair, definitely a settlement!

jokes.text: Tom's defense of Ron's 'overthrowing the government' talk: 'He's always talking about overthrowing the government, but he never does that.'
jokes.setup: After the perjury debacle, the court has damning evidence about Ron.
jokes.punchline: Tom's casual defense reveals that 'overthrowing the government' is a normal, everyday part of Ron's rhetoric — treated as harmless by Tom because it's so consistent.
jokes.explanation: A great Ron character joke delivered through Tom — the implication that Ron's anti-government rhetoric is so constant that it's become background noise is excellent. 'He never does that' as a defense is simultaneously the best and worst defense possible. Captures Ron's libertarianism as a comedic trait.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? Never mind. My story is boring.

jokes.text: Ron's statement: '...he dropped so quickly I thought he was diving towards the ground. I regret nothing. The end.'
jokes.setup: Ron is given the opportunity to make a statement in his defense.
jokes.punchline: 'I regret nothing. The end.' — Ron concludes his testimony with serene finality, treating what is clearly a damaging admission as a point of pride.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Ron Swanson moment. His entire testimony is an honest account that is catastrophically bad for his case, delivered with the composure of a man who has no regrets. 'I regret nothing. The end.' is a perfect closing statement — both the funniest and worst possible thing to say in court. 'He dropped so quickly I thought he was diving toward the ground' is also an excellent piece of Ron deadpan. The 'The End' as a formal closing is pure Ron — treating his testimony as a completed narrative.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I may have stolen this key from the city offices, but I knew you'd need it.

jokes.text: Jamm: 'You got jammed by your own team. Self-Jamm!'
jokes.setup: Jamm has just witnessed Ron's testimony self-destruct.
jokes.punchline: 'Self-Jamm!' — Jamm invents a terminology for when someone is their own worst enemy, using his own name as a verb, which is peak Jamm vanity.
jokes.explanation: Jamm using his own name as a verb for self-defeat is a great character moment — the vanity of naming a phenomenon after yourself while gloating is deeply Jamm. 'Self-Jamm!' has good energy and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I know that was your key, but it was a symbolic gesture.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.line: Symbolic? That's my house key!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I understand, and I apologize, but sometimes you have to do things that are bigger than one person's immediate needs.

jokes.text: Ben, lucid for 20 minutes before more morphine, asks to see the key. Leslie: 'Oh, they wanted to get it engraved.' / 'The key is just a metaphor. The real key has been inside you all along.' / 'It was a setup, wasn't it?'
jokes.setup: Ben asks to see the key to the city. Leslie has to explain that they took it back.
jokes.punchline: Leslie resorts to 'the real key has been inside you all along' — a transparent platitude — and Ben immediately sees through it: 'It was a setup, wasn't it?'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's platitude pivot is a good comic beat — she tries to pivot to metaphor and Ben deflates it immediately. The reversal from Leslie's usual relentless optimism to a cover story is funny. Decent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Come on, let's just slip out the back.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Good idea. Nobody needs to know we were here.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.line: Hey! Ben Wyatt! The Ice Town guy!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh no...

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.line: Ice Town costs Ice Clown! Ha!

jokes.text: Ann and Chris at the fertility counselor: '58%, which as I'm saying it, sounds very clearly like we failed.'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to frame their score optimistically in front of the doctor.
jokes.punchline: Midway through her sentence, she realizes what she's saying and can't maintain the spin.
jokes.explanation: A good self-correcting observation joke — the humor is in Ann's real-time processing of her own sentence. Well-constructed and delivered.

jokes.text: The free-association co-parenting exercise: 'Occupation?' / 'Teacher.' / 'Six-time Tour de France champion.'
jokes.setup: Doctor asks them to free-associate about their future child's occupation.
jokes.punchline: Ann says 'teacher' (reasonable); Chris says 'six-time Tour de France champion' — which is wildly specific and competitive, revealing his intense achievement-orientation even in parental fantasy.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke for Chris. 'Six-time Tour de France champion' as a parental dream is absurdly specific — not just 'champion' or 'athlete,' but SIX times, which reveals Chris's maximalism. The contrast with Ann's simple 'teacher' makes the joke land harder. This is what 8 looks like: deeply character-specific, structurally clean, genuinely surprising.

jokes.text: Doctor asks: 'Okay, I'm sorry, are you guys complete strangers? Is this one of those Craigslist father situations?'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann have given completely incompatible answers to every question, despite knowing each other well.
jokes.punchline: The doctor's deadpan 'is this one of those Craigslist father situations?' — implying their incompatibility is so total she assumes they just met — is the outside-view confirmation of the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Craigslist father situation' is a great specific cultural reference joke — the doctor's bafflement expressed through contemporary internet slang is unexpected and funny. The specificity of 'Craigslist' elevates it from a generic stranger-parents joke.

jokes.text: Ron reveals he stores his wealth in gold and palladium: 'I'm actually not sure how much money I have. But I do know how many pounds of money I have.'
jokes.setup: Tom and April worry about whether Ron can pay a huge settlement.
jokes.punchline: Ron casually reveals that he doesn't track his wealth in dollars but in physical weight — his money is literally in precious metal ingots, and he knows his fortune by the pound.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a top-tier Ron Swanson moment. The revelation that Ron doesn't know his dollar net worth but knows his pounds of money is perfectly constructed — it's specific enough to be surprising, utterly Ron, and reveals a whole hidden world of his life (bunker full of gold). The structure is perfect: the setup (can you pay?) leads to a reassurance that opens into the absurd reveal. Highly quotable and genuinely original.

jokes.text: Tom says he's 'definitely tweeting that to Drake to use in his next rhymes.'
jokes.setup: Tom reacts to Ron's 'pounds of money' revelation.
jokes.punchline: Tom's response is to immediately try to get Drake rap credit — turning Ron's stoic frontier philosophy into a hip-hop lyric opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Tom's celebrity name-dropping and the idea of getting Drake lyrical content from Ron Swanson is funny in the collision of worlds. Not exceptional craft but solid Tom character moment.

jokes.text: April: 'UGH, do we have to do something nice now?'
jokes.setup: Tom acknowledges they caused Ron's legal problem with their perjury.
jokes.punchline: April's visceral disgust at the prospect of doing something nice is a perfect, compact April moment.
jokes.explanation: Seven words perfectly encapsulating April's entire character. Her abhorrence of performing niceness, even when clearly warranted, is pure April. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: APRIL: 'UGH, do we have to do something nice now?'
jokes.setup: Tom and April feel guilty that their testimony hurt Ron's case and discuss making it right.
jokes.punchline: April's resignation to performing niceness — treating decency as an onerous obligation — is a perfect April line.
jokes.explanation: Short and perfect. April's horror at the prospect of doing something nice is well-compressed into one sentence. High character integration — this is quintessential April — and excellent economy.

jokes.text: Leslie to Mayor Stice: 'Can't you just give Ben a key to the city, here, now, in your office, where no one will know your shame? Sorry, babe.' / Ben: 'No worries. I love you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to negotiate a private key ceremony with the mayor.
jokes.punchline: Leslie calls out the mayor's shame directly ('where no one will know your shame'), then immediately apologizes to Ben for framing his hometown reconciliation as an act of concealed humiliation. Ben's 'No worries. I love you.' is a perfect non-reactive button.
jokes.explanation: A good double-beat — Leslie's diplomatic misstep (naming the shame explicitly) followed by her self-correction, with Ben's serene acceptance as the button. Shows Leslie's obliviousness and Ben's patience well.

jokes.text: Ben tries to feed the mayor's bronze eagle statue, thinking it's real.
jokes.setup: Ben is still slightly loopy from morphine and spots the mayor's decorative eagle.
jokes.punchline: He attempts to feed it — only to be corrected 'It's bronze, babe.' The visual of Ben earnestly feeding a statue is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A good morphine-Ben visual gag. The residual drug confusion leading him to feed a bronze statue is funny and grounded in the established character state. 'It's bronze, babe' is a good Leslie straight-man line.

jokes.text: Ann's confessional: 'I bought 12 babies and then I immediately abandoned them at a Kroger's.' [Beat] Chris: 'Look, we can use anything as a baby. I mean, we could use this mug.'
jokes.setup: Ann is devastated about leaving the eggs at the grocery store.
jokes.punchline: Chris's immediate pivot to 'we could use this mug' as a baby substitute is the optimist solution — treating any object as an adequate baby metaphor.
jokes.explanation: Chris's 'use a mug' solution is a good character beat — his problem-solving positivity applied to a fundamentally absurd problem. The mug-as-baby is funny in its randomness. Works as a callback to the egg abandonment.

jokes.text: Chris's 'new quiz' for Ann: a single question — 'Will you love our child and work hard to see that he or she has a good life?'
jokes.setup: Chris proposes another compatibility quiz after all the discouraging results
jokes.punchline: The quiz is a single, sincere yes/no question — a pointed contrast to the elaborate quantitative test they failed
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the compatibility quiz running gag — replacing elaborate algorithmic assessment with a single sincere question. Emotionally satisfying and structurally sound as a running gag conclusion. The comedy is in the contrast with everything that preceded it.

jokes.text: Chris shows Ann a new quiz with just one question: 'Will you love our child and work hard to see that he or she has a good life?'
jokes.setup: Ann is discouraged by all the compatibility tests. Chris returns with 'one more.'
jokes.punchline: The 'quiz' is just one sincere question — stripping away the algorithmic compatibility scoring for a simple emotional truth. The joke is that this is both absurdly simple and genuinely the right answer to their problem.
jokes.explanation: Plays more as warm sitcom resolution than comedy, but the comedy is in Chris reframing the entire quiz arc as a single earnest question. Works better as character beat than pure joke.

jokes.text: Chris proposes to Ann while holding a coffee mug as a stand-in baby: 'You know there's nothing in there yet, right?' / 'Yes, sorry.'
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann have decided to have a baby together; Chris holds up a mug as a symbolic gesture
jokes.punchline: Ann points out the mug is empty — 'You know there's nothing in there yet, right?' — and Chris's sincere apology for symbolically presenting an empty mug as their future child
jokes.explanation: A sweet, light callback to Ann's earlier 'we could use this mug' suggestion. The joke is in Chris's earnest symbolism being deflated by Ann's literal observation. Warm and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Jamm is mid-story about 'Johnny Cougar Mellencamp' and 'yabbos' when Tom and April interrupt.
jokes.setup: Jamm is interrupted mid-anecdote.
jokes.punchline: The fragment we hear — Jamm was telling a story involving John Cougar Mellencamp and women's breasts ('yabbos') at a music festival — is perfectly calibrated sleaze. 'WHAT THE HELL? That was important.' is the button.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's interrupted sleazy anecdote is a good character beat — the fact that he considers this 'important' is the joke. 'Yabbos' appearing a second time establishes it as Jamm's word.

jokes.text: Tom dramatically fakes injury when Jamm snatches a document: 'OW! My wrist! You twisted my arm like a maniac!' / 'My face! Is my face still there? What happened to my knees?'
jokes.setup: Jamm grabs the perjury document from Tom. Tom sees an opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately performs catastrophic injury — the escalation from 'my wrist' to 'my face' to 'my knees' despite none of them being touched is a perfect escalating hypochondria performance.
jokes.explanation: Tom's fake injury escalation is excellent physical comedy on paper — the rapid anatomical expansion ('wrist... face... knees?') with zero logical connection to what actually happened is very funny. 'Is my face still there?' is a particularly great line. The group's straight-man response ('Oh my God, Tom, are you okay?') and Jamm's growing panic add to it. Great structure.

jokes.text: 'Hurry, Tom, let's get you into surgery!' — Leslie dramatically rushes Tom out as the scam concludes.
jokes.setup: Jamm has agreed to drop the suit to prevent further liability exposure.
jokes.punchline: Leslie commits fully to the fake injury narrative: 'Hurry, Tom, let's get you into surgery!' — even though Tom is fine — is a great button on the scam sequence.
jokes.explanation: A good button on the scam sequence. Leslie's full commitment to the fake-injury narrative is character-consistent (she commits to plans) and funny as an exit line.

jokes.text: Tom on the phone: 'Yeah, it's me. We got Jammed.'
jokes.setup: After successfully defeating Jamm's lawsuit via the counter-threat.
jokes.punchline: Tom uses 'Jammed' (from Jamm's name) to mean they successfully jammed/defeated Jamm — a callback to 'Self-Jamm' and a reversal of Jamm's own terminology.
jokes.explanation: A tight callback that turns Jamm's own vanity-vocabulary against him. 'We got Jammed' means they won — and echoes Jamm's earlier 'Self-Jamm.' Economical and satisfying.

jokes.text: Ben's childhood fishing story: 'One time, our boat almost tipped over, but then it didn't.' / 'That's not a great story.' / 'Yeah, I had a pretty uneventful childhood.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells Stephanie a memory from fishing in the lake.
jokes.punchline: The story has no climax — 'almost tipped, but didn't' is the entirety of it. Ben's self-aware response — 'yeah, I had a pretty uneventful childhood' — is both sad and funny.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed anti-story joke. The setup creates the expectation of an anecdote, then delivers nothing — 'but then it didn't' is the perfect anti-climax. Ben's self-assessment 'I had a pretty uneventful childhood' is a good emotionally honest punchline that works on multiple levels given the Ice Town context. Economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: Leslie stole the key to the city from Mayor Stice's office: 'I stole it from Mayor Stice's office. Screw that guy. You should have it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie presents Ben with a key to the city despite the mayor refusing to give him one.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Leslie — Leslie Knope, devoted public servant — simply stole it, delivered with cheerful defiance ('screw that guy') is a great character subversion.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's casual theft on behalf of Ben — against her every instinct as a civil servant — is a wonderful character moment. 'Screw that guy. You should have it.' delivered with matter-of-fact warmth is the perfect Leslie-in-love beat. The comedy comes from the character doing something completely against type for love.

jokes.text: Ben doesn't want the key: 'I mean, I love Partridge, but I have Pawnee now. And I have you.' They throw the key into the lake, and a fisherman immediately yells: 'Hey, lake's not a garbage can, pal!' / 'Yeah, sorry, it was symbolic.' / 'Is that Ben Wyatt? Get the hell out of here, Ice Town!' / 'RUN!'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie have a sweet moment throwing the key into the lake as a symbol of moving on.
jokes.punchline: The fisherman immediately ruins the moment with an environmental complaint, followed by Ben being recognized and shouted at — a perfect comedic deflation of the sentimental scene, with 'it was symbolic' as a great straight-faced response.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and an excellent comedic ending. The structure is perfect: emotional payoff (Ben moving on from Partridge), interrupted by the practical complaint (lake's not a garbage can), followed by recognition and immediate hostility. The escalation from 'symbolic' to 'ICE TOWN! GET OUT!' is beautifully timed. The episode ends on Ben and Leslie running from Partridge, which is both funny and thematically right. The specificity of 'it was symbolic' as a genuine attempt to explain to the fisherman is a great character beat.

jokes.text: Ben throws the key into the lake; a Partridge local yells 'Hey, lake's not a garbage can, pal.' / Ben: 'Yeah, sorry, it was symbolic.' / Local: 'Is that Ben Wyatt? Get the hell out of here, Ice Town!'
jokes.setup: Ben decides to throw the key into the lake as a meaningful gesture of releasing his Ice Town guilt
jokes.punchline: The symbolic gesture is immediately misread as littering; Ben explains it's symbolic; the local doesn't care — then recognizes Ben and reverts to hostility
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured three-beat closing joke. The symbolic moment is punctured by a prosaic littering complaint, deflating the emotional climax. Ben's earnest explanation ('It was symbolic') is then further undercut by the local recognizing him and driving them away. The 'Run! Run!' as a closing image is both funny and a perfect encapsulation of Ben's relationship with Partridge. Strong structure and rewatch value as the episode's closing comedic moment.

tmdb_overview: Leslie accompanies Ben on a trip to his hometown which has offered him a key to the city. Ron deals with a lawsuit filed against him by Councilman Jamm. Ann and Chris take a parenting compatibility quiz.
insight: Absurdist escalation drives a modest 60-joke hour into elite territory at exactly 80.1.
